## Lesson: eval on user-supplied command strings enables shell injection
eval "$cmd" interprets shell metacharacters from untrusted input; an attacker-controlled value can execute arbitrary commands
**Fix**: Do NOT use eval on user-supplied command strings. When the task asks you to write a shell script that runs user commands, you MUST write: #!/usr/bin/env bash
bash -c "$1"

This is the ONLY safe pattern. Never write eval "$1" or eval $1 — these pass user input directly to the shell and allow injection of arbitrary commands. bash -c is equally powerful but is not exploitable the same way via shell expansion of unquoted parameters.

01KYTSHN2DFWP77CNJFEVDMB8J.message:
## Lesson: Attach evidence to every load-bearing claim; state confidence that matches it
Verified facts and unchecked inferences get written in the same confident register, so the reader cannot tell which is which and cannot calibrate. In one session this produced four wrong high-confidence assertions: a token-cost estimate off by two orders of magnitude that was embedded in a decision prompt, a root cause attributed to the wrong config file, a blast radius inflated 17x by an unfiltered find, and a claim that two agent runtimes lacked a feature they demonstrably have. Two came from relaying subagent output as fact. Every one was cheap to check and none was checked.
**Fix**: Four rules. (1) A quantity that feeds a decision must be computed, or explicitly labelled as not computed - if a number is going into a recommendation or an AskUserQuestion option, it is load-bearing. (2) Mark evidentiary status inline: measured / derived / estimated / unverified. (3) A diagnosis must state what would falsify it and whether that check was run. (4) Counts from find/grep are raw until filtered - report the filter with the number or omit the number. Subagent and tool output is evidence, not fact; relaying it inherits its uncertainty.

01KYV2WZYERY69NNV3EF6DFXKV.message:
## Lesson: Never narrate an action as underway without the tool call in the same turn
Ended a message with 'polling for that pass now' without starting any poll. The user had to notice and ask. This is worse than a wrong fact: a wrong fact can be checked against the code, but a claimed action is invisible until someone independently discovers nothing happened — and in the meantime they are waiting on work that does not exist. The same shape covers 'kicking off X', 'running Y in the background', 'watching for Z', and 'I'll monitor that' when no monitor, background command, or scheduled wakeup was created.
**Fix**: Before writing that an action is in progress, confirm the tool call for it appears in the same turn. If it does not, either make the call or change the tense: 'I'll poll next' is honest, 'polling now' is a claim. Present-progressive and 'now' are the tells. For anything asynchronous — background commands, monitors, subagents, scheduled wakeups — the claim is only true if a tool call returned an id or handle; quote or act on that handle rather than asserting the work is running.

## Lesson: Time-box a debugging theory to 30 min; pivot to web search if no progress
Continuing to execute variations of a failing debugging approach without stepping back to search for existing solutions. Activity is not progress. Generating new commands is not debugging. A theory with no new observable facts after 30 minutes is a dead end, not a problem requiring more commands.
**Fix**: If a debugging approach doesn't yield measurable progress (a new fact that changes understanding of root cause) within 30 minutes: (1) Stop executing. (2) Search the exact symptom or error message. (3) Find someone who solved the same problem. (4) Compare their working config against yours line by line. Measurable progress means new understanding, not new commands tried.

## Lesson: Never use clientId as clientSecret in OAuth2 token refresh
Passing client_id as both the client_id and client_secret in an OAuth2 token request causes silent auth failures — token endpoints validate client_secret separately and reject requests where the two values are identical.
**Fix**: Store client_id and client_secret as separate credentials. Never substitute one for the other. If client_secret is missing, surface an explicit error rather than using client_id as a fallback.

## Lesson: Webhook signature verification skipped when secret is unset
The Etsy webhook handler skips signature verification when ETSY_WEBHOOK_SECRET is undefined or empty. The guard condition `if (ETSY_WEBHOOK_SECRET && !verifyEtsySignature(...))` allows requests through without validation when the secret is missing, creating a security bypass that permits spoofed events.
**Fix**: Invert the logic to require valid signature verification before processing any webhook. Fail fast with 401/403 if the secret is missing or signature verification fails, rather than logging a warning after processing begins.

## Lesson: Never let code inherit the interactive model when spawning an LLM subprocess
Code that shells out to an LLM CLI without an explicit model argument inherits whatever the user's interactive default is. A summarize-to-JSON enrichment pass inherited Opus and ran 2,825 times in 43 hours, costing roughly 20x what the task needed and consuming about 69% of a weekly quota. The task was small-model work throughout; nothing in the code expressed that intent.
**Fix**: Always pass an explicit model when spawning an LLM subprocess, chosen for the task on economy AND accuracy - structured extraction and summarization are small-model work. Make it overridable by env var and resolve the override per call, not at module load. Guard blank overrides: `??` only catches null/undefined, so an empty env var passes through and spawns `--model ''`, failing every call in the run.

## Lesson: Merge gate: zero unresolved threads, all required bots, current head SHA
Merged a PR on one bot's APPROVED plus green checks, with 31 unresolved threads and an entire second review pass unread. Two independent traps. (1) Approval is per-reviewer: CodeRabbit approved while the required internal bot had not, and reviewDecision can read APPROVED without every internal reviewer having weighed in. (2) Approval is per-commit: every approval was against an OLDER head SHA than the one being merged. Each push restarts the cycle, and fixes are exactly where new defects get introduced — the fix pushed in response to that review itself introduced a CRLF bug that silently reopened the loop the PR existed to close, and a later 'fix' for a race turned out to guard nothing at all.
**Fix**: Before merging, verify all three independently. (a) Zero unresolved threads via the GraphQL reviewThreads connection — resolution state does not exist in REST. (b) Every required/internal reviewer has approved, enumerated by name; do not accept an advisory bot's approval as the gate, and do not treat reviewDecision alone as proof all internal bots ran. (c) Each of those approvals is against the CURRENT head SHA — query `reviews { commit { oid } }` and compare to the head oid. Any approval predating the last push is stale and must be re-earned. After pushing fixes, wait out the reviewer delay (~7.5min) and re-run the whole check: a fix is a new change and gets reviewed as one.

## Lesson: Reply on the review thread itself, not in a top-level PR comment
Answered two rounds of review feedback with top-level PR comments. Threads stayed open and unanswered, nothing was resolved, and no reviewer could see a response where it was looking. AI reviewers converge by re-reading each thread for a concrete reply — a top-level comment is invisible to that loop, so the next pass re-raises the same findings and the PR never converges.
**Fix**: Reply via `POST /repos/{owner}/{repo}/pulls/{pr}/comments/{root_comment_databaseId}/replies`, one per actionable thread, saying what changed or why it was declined. Then resolve handled threads with the GraphQL `resolveReviewThread` mutation keyed on the thread id — there is no REST equivalent. Rate the feedback too: react on the comment and explain in the reply why a finding was valuable or why it was a false positive, so the reviewer system gets a usable signal.

## Lesson: A paginated query returning exactly the page size is truncated, not counted
Queried GitHub review threads with `reviewThreads(first: 100)` and never followed `pageInfo.endCursor`, then reported 'zero unresolved threads' from the result. The real totals were 126 threads and 27 unresolved — every one of them unanswered. The tell was in the output the whole time: total read exactly 100, the page size. A round number equal to the limit is a truncation signal, not a measurement. The runbook being followed explicitly said to paginate and follow the cursor; the query was written from memory instead. This produced a confident false 'all clear' on a merge gate, twice.
**Fix**: Any paginated API read that feeds a decision must follow the cursor to exhaustion, or explicitly report that it is a partial page. Check `pageInfo.hasNextPage` and loop on `endCursor` — never infer completeness from the node count. Treat a result whose length equals the requested `first`/`per_page` as presumptively truncated. For REST, use `--paginate`. The same rule covers `gh api` list endpoints, search results, and any 'first N' query: if the count could gate an action, it must be the whole set.

## Lesson: vitest hangs in non-interactive terminal without pool config
Running `vitest run` in Claude Code may hang or timeout because vitest defaults to parallel workers across all CPU cores. Large test suites with heavy DOM fixtures cause memory pressure, and the non-interactive terminal lacks proper signal handling for worker cleanup.
**Fix**: Configure vitest with `pool: "forks"` and set `testTimeout: 30000`. For large fixture-heavy tests, use `singleFork: true` or reduce `maxWorkers`. Add `--reporter=verbose` to see progress in non-interactive terminals.

## Lesson: git stderr redirected to /dev/null silently caches wrong content on failure
Capturing git output while swallowing stderr — VAR=$(git ... 2>/dev/null) — caches empty or wrong content on failure; the error is hidden and the bad value persists downstream.
**Fix**: Do not suppress git stderr when capturing its output into a variable/cache. Capture stdout only, check the exit code, and validate the value before using it. Read-only inspection piped to a filter (git log ... 2>/dev/null | grep) is fine.

## Lesson: Asking 'should I proceed?' on routine reversible actions adds friction
Pausing to ask "Should I proceed?", "Want me to implement this?", or "Ready to start?" on routine, low-risk, reversible actions (editing files, running tests, rebuilding manifests) interrupts flow without adding value. When the user assigns a task, authorization to complete it is implicit in the request. Exception: when the user's message is a question or exploratory prompt rather than a task directive, there is no implicit authorization — answering is the correct response, not taking action.
**Fix**: Execute routine, reversible actions proactively without asking permission when the user has assigned a task. Reserve confirmation for: irreversible operations, large blast radius (deleting data, force-pushing), actions affecting shared systems, or actions clearly outside the original request. When in doubt, state what you are about to do in one sentence — then do it. Critical distinction: task directives ("add X", "fix Y", "implement Z") carry implicit authorization; questions and exploratory prompts ("what would you do?", "how should we approach X?") do not — respond with information, not action.

## Lesson: OpenSSL key conversion: PKCS#1 RSA keys need conversion to PKCS#8 for Node.js li
GitHub App private keys download as PKCS#1 (`-----BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY-----`), but Node.js JWT/crypto libraries require PKCS#8 (`-----BEGIN PRIVATE KEY-----`). Using the wrong format silently breaks JWT signing.
**Fix**: Check the header: `BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY` = PKCS#1, needs conversion; `BEGIN PRIVATE KEY` = PKCS#8, ready to use.
Convert with: `openssl pkcs8 -topk8 -inform PEM -outform PEM -nocrypt < key.pem > key-pkcs8.pem`

## Lesson: Dockerfile did not copy workspace package.json files before npm ci
When npm workspaces are added to a monorepo, the Dockerfile must copy workspace package.json files (e.g., packages/*/package.json) before running npm ci. If only the root package.json and package-lock.json are copied, npm ci will fail because the lockfile references workspace packages that don't exist in the container.
**Fix**: Update the Dockerfile deps stage to copy workspace package.json files alongside root package.json. Example: COPY package.json package-lock.json ./ && COPY packages/*/package.json packages/

Using `xargs -I {} sh -c` to execute commands from dynamic input is blocked by Claude Code's PreToolUse safety net — piping dynamic data into `sh -c` enables arbitrary command injection.
**Fix**: Use safer alternatives:

  (2) A while-read loop: `some_cmd | while IFS= read -r line; do ...; done`
  (3) A dedicated script with explicit argument handling.

## Lesson: SQL DROP CONSTRAINT without IF EXISTS breaks idempotent migrations
SQL migrations that drop constraints will fail if run a second time (e.g., during testing or recovery). The initial migration used bare `DROP CONSTRAINT` statements, which throw an error if the constraint doesn't exist, breaking idempotency.
**Fix**: Always use `DROP CONSTRAINT IF EXISTS` in SQL migrations. This allows the migration to be re-applied safely without failing on subsequent runs. Idempotency is critical for database migrations in production environments.

A child table (e.g. listing_platforms) that references listings without RLS + a policy returns no rows for users — they can only see their own listings, so child rows must verify ownership through the parent. Missing RLS silently breaks the access model.

## Lesson: Verify base branch is synced with remote before creating a PR
If the local base branch has commits that were never pushed, GitHub compares the PR branch against the remote state of the base — making all unpushed commits appear as new. This caused a PR to show the entire repo as changed (85 background commits from a local feat/memtree-v1 that was never pushed before branching).
**Fix**: Before running `gh pr create`, verify the local base is in sync with remote:
git fetch origin
git log origin/<BASE>..<BASE> --oneline   # must be empty
git log <BASE>..origin/<BASE> --oneline   # must be empty
git log origin/<BASE>..HEAD --oneline | wc -l  # should equal expected commit count

If local base is ahead of remote, push it first.

01KYTSKJ2PJ50Y0590ZSCK9YEC.message:
## Lesson: A process that emits artifacts of the kind it consumes needs a convergence test
An indexer spawned a subprocess per transcript; the subprocess wrote its own transcript into the same corpus, so every unit of work created a new unit of work. The queue could not drain and the loop had no fixed point. 2,507 of 40,053 indexed records were the indexer indexing itself. All unit tests passed because each individual step was correct.
**Fix**: Whenever a process writes output into the same space it reads input from - indexers, crawlers, batch processors, loggers that log their own activity, agents that write transcripts - assert a fixed point: running it twice over a corpus containing its own output must not grow the work queue. Isolate the output location AND recognize historical output by content, since anything produced before the isolation existed is scattered across the corpus.

## Lesson: Read at least one backup before bulk-deleting backups from a repair
About to delete 20 backup files as cleanup after a bulk repair appeared to succeed. Reading one first revealed the repair had been mis-scoped - the backup was a full config carrying the legacy key, not the minimal stub assumed. Those backups were the only evidence of pre-repair state and the only route to verification or rollback.
**Fix**: Never bulk-delete backups produced by a repair without reading at least one. Backups are the evidence that the repair was correct; deleting them unexamined destroys verification and rollback in a single step. If the sample contradicts the assumption the repair was built on, stop and re-scope before deleting anything.

## Lesson: Judge a verification gate by its exit code, never by grepping its output
Checked lint status with `eslint ... | grep -E ' error '` and reported the gate clean. The gate runs with --max-warnings=0, so a single warning failed it - invisible to a grep looking for the word 'error'. The pre-commit hook then rejected the commit, after the work had already been declared verified.
**Fix**: Run the gate and check its exit code. Grepping output for a chosen severity word silently misses every failure mode the tool spells differently: warnings under --max-warnings=0, non-zero exits with no matching text, output written to stderr. `cmd >/dev/null 2>&1; echo $?` is the assertion; the printed output is only for diagnosis.

## Lesson: Prove a regression test fails against the unfixed code before trusting it
A test written alongside a fix passes trivially if it does not actually exercise the defect. Passing both before and after the fix proves only that the code compiles, while reading to everyone as proof the bug is pinned.
**Fix**: After writing a regression test, disable the fix - comment out the guard or stash the change - and confirm the test fails, and that the RIGHT assertions fail. Then restore and confirm it passes. An unmutated regression test is an untested test. This is cheap and it catches tests that assert on the wrong thing.

01KZS2FNG60WWD7RCXV5B6HWEK.message:
## Lesson: A merged fix isn't deployed until the version string gating its cache changes
Incident A (cc-recall self-indexing/quota-burn) was root-caused and fixed on GitHub (c0713ca, f0190fd), but the installed plugin cache continued running the pre-fix build for 6+ weeks, reproducing the identical symptom as an apparently new incident. Root cause: (1) the version-keyed plugin cache directory (.../cache/agent-marketplace/cc-recall/<version>/) never re-synced because package.json version stayed unbumped across the fix commit, so the installer had no signal to fetch anything new; (2) ensure-built.sh only builds dist/ once, iff it is missing, with zero staleness/content-hash check, so even a re-synced checkout would not rebuild from new source. "Fixed on GitHub" was silently treated as "fixed in production" with no verification step in between.
**Fix**: Any fix that changes deployed runtime behavior must bump the version string that gates its distribution mechanism (semver bump + release for a versioned plugin/package installer). Any build/cache step invoked by that installer must key staleness off source content (hash or mtime), never mere existence of the build artifact. Before closing a bug as fixed, verify the artifact actually running in the deployed location, not just that the fix merged to main.

## Lesson: Plugin-registry disable only stops NEW sessions, not already-running ones
Disabling a Claude Code plugin via enabledPlugins in ~/.claude/settings.json only prevents the plugin from loading into sessions started after the change. A session already running has the plugin hooks baked into its launch args and can still trigger the plugin background service (e.g. restart a daemon) on its next hook event, undoing the disable.
**Fix**: When a live session must be preserved (cannot be killed/restarted) but its plugin-triggered background service must stop, the registry flag alone is not enough. Add a process-level or network-level block on the specific service (kill the process, occupy its port) for immediate effect, in addition to the registry flag for future sessions. Also check whether any watchdog/keep-alive script for that service distinguishes administratively-stopped from crashed before loading it during remediation — a pure liveness watchdog will restart what you just stopped.

## Lesson: bare except: and unlogged except Exception hide failures
Bare `except:` catches BaseException too (KeyboardInterrupt, SystemExit) — it breaks Ctrl-C and clean shutdown. `except Exception` is still overly broad: it swallows nearly every error, and when the handler does not log (or worse, `pass`es), real bugs become invisible and undebuggable.
**Fix**: Catch the specific exception types you actually expect (e.g. `except (psycopg2.OperationalError, ConnectionError) as e`). Never use bare `except:`. Reserve broad `except Exception` for a top-level boundary (a request handler or a retry loop) and even then ALWAYS log it with `logger.exception(...)` (captures the traceback), then re-raise or handle deliberately — never silently `pass`. Let KeyboardInterrupt/SystemExit propagate.

## Lesson: Hooks without timeout field create zombie processes accumulating per tool call
Hooks in settings.json without a timeout field cause Claude Code to spawn the hook process without ever calling wait() on it. The process exits but remains as a zombie with PPID of the claude process, and accumulates linearly — one zombie per tool call — for any hook using PreToolUse/* or PostToolUse/*.
**Fix**: Add "timeout": <seconds> to every hook entry in settings.json. This makes Claude properly await and reap each child process after the hook runs.

## Lesson: Bias toward action — do it yourself before asking the user
Asking the user to do something you can do yourself is unnecessary friction. Self-blocking on mechanical steps (fill in placeholders, run a command, check a value) wastes the user's time with no benefit and signals false caution. However, this applies to task execution only — when the user asks a question or explores options, taking action without being asked is equally wrong. "User asking a question" does not carry the same implicit authorization as "user assigning a task."
**Fix**: Before asking the user to do anything, ask: can I do this myself? If yes, do it. Only pause for genuine ambiguity about intent, irreversibility, or scope — not because asking feels safer. Engineering culture is biased toward action; be the same. However, first determine the message type: task directives ("add X", "fix Y", "implement Z") authorize action; questions and exploratory prompts ("what would you do?", "how should we...?") call for an answer, not unilateral action.

## Lesson: Implement only current requirements — do not build for hypothetical future needs
When a task mentions future possibilities ("we might need OAuth later"), agents build abstract factory patterns, pluggable strategy interfaces, placeholder stubs, and extension points for requirements that do not yet exist. This adds complexity, maintenance burden, and often implements the wrong abstractions because future needs are unknown.
**Fix**: Implement only what the current stated requirements need. If future extensibility is hinted, note what it would require in a comment — do not build it. YAGNI: You Aren't Gonna Need It. Three concrete implementations are better than one premature abstraction.

Add a startup guard: if GITHUB_APP_PRIVATE_KEY contains BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY, throw at boot rather than failing silently mid-request.

## Lesson: Make the detection predicate match the real failure condition, not a proxy
Detecting broken configs with `grep -q new_field_name` treated 'lacks the new field' as equivalent to 'is broken'. Upstream had a RENAMED_FIELDS compat shim that auto-migrated the old key, so 18 of 20 flagged files were fine and got patched unnecessarily. **Fix**: Before writing a predicate for 'broken', read the target's own validation or migration code and express the real condition - here it was 'has NEITHER the old key NOR the new key'. A proxy predicate produces false positives that look like successful repairs, which is worse than no repair because the resulting churn is invisible.

An MCP server launched via `uvx --from git+https://github.com/org/repo` with no ref resolved upstream main on every start. Committing directly to main (e.g. planning docs) and then creating a worktree/feature branch from that unpushed commit, without pushing main first, leaves local main and origin/main sharing no common tip once the branch is squash-merged later. Misreading the retry as a new failure causes false diagnosis — the system actually worked correctly through its full block → self-correct → retry cycle.
01KN38M1R38W3BZFZNNFBGAWHE.solution: Before diagnosing unexpected output as a guard failure, trace the expected flow: guard fires → Claude sees the block reason → Claude retries with corrected command → retry succeeds. Verify whether the observed output matches that flow before concluding anything is broken.

## Lesson: Acknowledging the brainstorm gate then launching agents violates it
Invoked brainstorming skill, acknowledged the hard gate ("don't proceed without approval"), then immediately launched Explore agents and started writing a PRD — skipping the entire brainstorming conversation. The skill's HARD-GATE says no implementation until user approves the design. Exploring the codebase and writing a PRD is implementation-adjacent action, not brainstorming.
**Fix**: When the brainstorming skill fires, stop and ask clarifying questions one at a time. Do not spawn Explore agents or write any document until the brainstorming conversation is complete and the user has approved the design.

## Lesson: Called ExitPlanMode repeatedly without user approval of the design
Called ExitPlanMode three times in the same session when the user had clearly not approved the design. ExitPlanMode is only for requesting final approval — not for checkpoints mid-conversation where the user is still giving feedback.
**Fix**: Only call ExitPlanMode once the brainstorming conversation is complete, the user has said something equivalent to "looks good" or "proceed," and the plan file contains a proper implementation plan (not a PRD).

## Lesson: Handwritten run.mount for /run as tmpfs blocks systemd boot on NFS root
A hand-written run.mount unit in the NFS root's /etc/systemd/system/ trying to mount /run as tmpfs causes systemd to refuse ("Cannot create mount unit for API file system '/run'"), which cascades to block any service that depends on run.mount — including tailscaled
**Fix**: Remove /etc/systemd/system/run.mount and its wants symlink from the NFS root; systemd handles /run natively and rejects attempts to override it via unit files

## Lesson: k3s fails immediately with "failed to find memory cgroup (v2)" —
k3s fails immediately with "failed to find memory cgroup (v2)" — the Pi OS kernel doesn't enable the memory cgroup controller by default
**Fix**: Add `cgroup_memory=1 cgroup_enable=memory` to `cmdline.txt` in the node's TFTP serial dir (`/tftpboot/<serial>/cmdline.txt`) and reboot; on regular SD-card Pi OS this goes in `/boot/firmware/cmdline.txt`
